Cytochrome P450 enzymes - responsible for phase I metabolism of drugs and by making them more polar for excretion in the urine. UGT enzymes - responsible for phase II metabolism of drugs by conjugating them to clear out molecules such as glucuronic acid.  In the case of paracetamol, it is the cytochrome P450 enzymes that produce the toxic NAPBQI (n-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine) as a byproduct of phase I metabolism.  Hepatic glutathione - NAPBQI is quenched by hepatic glutathione in a normal dose of paracetamol however in an overdose, glutathione stores are depleted and more NAPBQI-induced hepatocyte necrosis occurs. n-acetylcysteine (NAC) - is used as a treatment for paracetamol overdose as it has a similar structure to cysteine an amino acid and replenishes hepatic glutathione levels.  n-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPBQI) - this is actually produced by the cytochrome P450 enzymes in the case of a paracetamol overdose and is the toxic compound that causes liver damage. NAC is used to inactivate this compound.

C is the correct answer Na+ is reabsorbed in the PCT via transport with organic molecules (e.g glucose) in the lumen. It is also exchanged with H+ secreted by the PCT cells into the lumen, and in exchange for HCO3- taken into the cell in solution. This is important in acid/base homeostasis. Na+ is then reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb via the Na+/K+2Cl- anti-porter. This is electrically important as as more posative charge is removed from the tubule, there is more negative potential inside the lumen which in turn means more Ca2+ and to a lesser extent, magnessium, is drawn out of the blood into the tubular fluid. This is important in Calcium homeostasis. Finally, in the DCT Na+ is reabsorbed via the Na+/Cl- co-transporter. Here it is exchanged with H+ from the blood into the tubule in exchange for HCO3- taken out into the blood cells. This is important in acid/base homeostasis.
